# Count deer observations by year
annual_counts <- as.data.frame(
  table(df_deer_clean$year)
)

# Rename columns
names(annual_counts) <- c("Year", "Observations")

# Convert year and count to numeric
annual_counts$Year <- as.integer(
  as.character(annual_counts$Year)
)

annual_counts$Observations <- as.integer(
  annual_counts$Observations
)

# View the summary table
annual_counts
##    Year Observations
## 1  2010           12
## 2  2011           15
## 3  2012           19
## 4  2013           40
## 5  2014           47
## 6  2015           77
## 7  2016          150
## 8  2017          291
## 9  2018          452
## 10 2019          740
## 11 2020         1048
# Figure 1: Annual white-tailed deer observations in NC

plot(
  annual_counts$Year,
  annual_counts$Observations,
  type = "o",
  pch = 16,
  col = "steelblue",
  lwd = 2,
  xlab = "Year",
  ylab = "Number of observations",
  main = "Annual White-tailed Deer Observations in North Carolina",
  xaxt = "n"
)

axis(
  1,
  at = 2010:2020,
  labels = 2010:2020
)

Figure 1. Annual White-tailed Deer Observations in North Carolina (2010–2020)

Question: How did the number of recorded white-tailed deer observations change from 2010 to 2020? Observed pattern: The annual number of observations increased (12 records in 2010 to 1,048 in 2020). Units: Number of iNaturalist observation records per year. Limitation: The observed numbers do not equate to the actual number of deer populations. This trend may merely indicate an increase in people’s participation on the iNaturalist platform, rather than an actual growth in the deer population.

# Load North Carolina county boundaries
nc_map <- st_read("data/processed/NC_map_joined.shp")
## Reading layer `NC_map_joined' from data source 
##   `/Users/huangyiping/KalsiGivensHuangYang/Scripts/data/processed/NC_map_joined.shp' 
##   using driver `ESRI Shapefile'
## Simple feature collection with 100 features and 21 fields
## Geometry type: MULTIPOLYGON
## Dimension:     XY
## Bounding box:  xmin: -84.32187 ymin: 33.84232 xmax: -75.46062 ymax: 36.58812
## Geodetic CRS:  NAD83
# Convert deer coordinates into spatial points
deer_sf <- st_as_sf(
  df_deer_clean,
  coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  crs = 4326,
  remove = FALSE
)

# Match the coordinate system of the county map
deer_sf <- st_transform(deer_sf, st_crs(NC_map))

# Assign each deer observation to a county
deer_county <- st_join(
  deer_sf,
  NC_map[, c("NAME", "GEOID")],
  join = st_within,
  left = TRUE
)

# Preview the results
head(st_drop_geometry(deer_county)[, c("id", "NAME", "GEOID")])
## # A tibble: 6 × 3
##       id NAME      GEOID
##    <dbl> <chr>     <chr>
## 1  18471 Brunswick 37019
## 2  24092 Pender    37141
## 3  86366 Orange    37135
## 4 117764 Stokes    37169
## 5 246028 Robeson   37155
## 6 325785 Dare      37055
# Count deer observations by county
county_counts <- as.data.frame(
  table(deer_county$NAME)
)

# Rename columns
names(county_counts) <- c("NAME", "deer_count")

# Convert counts to numeric
county_counts$deer_count <- as.integer(county_counts$deer_count)

# Preview
head(county_counts)
##        NAME deer_count
## 1  Alamance         13
## 2 Alexander          1
## 3 Alleghany         20
## 4     Anson         16
## 5      Ashe         14
## 6     Avery        125
# Join deer counts to county boundaries
NC_map$deer_count <- county_counts$deer_count[
  match(NC_map$NAME, county_counts$NAME)
]

# Counties with no observations should have a count of zero
NC_map$deer_count[is.na(NC_map$deer_count)] <- 0

# Figure 2: Deer observations by county
plot(
  NC_map["deer_count"],
  main = "White-tailed Deer Observations by County in NC",
  pal = colorRampPalette(c("lightblue", "darkblue")),
  key.pos = 4,
  axes = FALSE,
  reset = FALSE
)

Figure 2. Spatial Distribution of White-tailed Deer Observations by County in North Carolina (2010–2020)

Question: How are white-tailed deer observations distributed across North Carolina counties? Observed pattern: Deer observations were unevenly distributed across counties. Units: Number of iNaturalist deer observation records per county. Limitation: Observation counts were not adjusted for county area or differences in observer. Additionally, 33 observations could not be assigned to a county and were excluded from this map. Therefore, higher observation counts do not necessarily indicate higher deer population density.

Three main findings

Temporal increase: Deer observation records increased substantially from 2010 to 2020, especially after 2016. Uneven spatial distribution: Observations were not evenly distributed across North Carolina counties. Concentration in a few counties: Wake (547), Orange (265), and Durham (188) together accounted for approximately 35% of county-assigned observations.

df_deer_spatial <- df_deer_clean %>%
  select(observed_on, year, longitude, latitude) %>%
  mutate(year = as.character(year)) %>%
  st_as_sf(coords = c('longitude','latitude'), crs=4269)
df_deer_in_NC <- st_join(df_deer_spatial, NC_map, join = st_within) %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  mutate(development = ifelse(HU_dif > 0, "yes", "no"),
         forest = ifelse(VEG_dif < 0, "dec", "inc")) %>%
  group_by(NAME, year, development, forest) %>%
  summarise(observation=n()) %>%
  ungroup(year, development, forest) %>%
  mutate(period = ifelse(year == "2016" | year == "2017" | year == "2018" | year == "2019", NA, 
                         ifelse(year == "2020", "after", "before")))
## `summarise()` has regrouped the output.
## ℹ Summaries were computed grouped by NAME, year, development, and forest.
## ℹ Output is grouped by NAME, year, and development.
## ℹ Use `summarise(.groups = "drop_last")` to silence this message.
## ℹ Use `summarise(.by = c(NAME, year, development, forest))` for per-operation
##   grouping (`?dplyr::dplyr_by`) instead.
map_deer_in_NC = ggplot() + 
  geom_sf(data = NC_map, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5, aes(fill = HU_dif)) + 
  geom_sf(data = df_deer_spatial%>%filter(year == "2010" | year == "2011" | year == "2012" | year == "2013" | year == "2014" | year == "2015"), color = "cyan", size = 0.5, alpha = 0.5, stroke = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low="darkblue", high="red") +
  labs(title = "Housing Unit Differnce by Counties with White-tailed Deer Observations before Development",
       fill = "Difference",
       caption = "Housing unit difference is calculated with data from 2020 subtracting data from 2010. Deer observation is the sum from 2010\nto 2015. The blue means unchanged or small increase of housing units in the counties, and the red means large increase.") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 11.5),
        plot.caption = element_text(hjust = 0))
map_deer_in_NC

Map 1-4

Question: How are white-tailed deer observations distributed across North Carolina counties with different development rate? Observed pattern: In terms of housing units, the deer observations before the development (2010-2015) spread out more than the once from 2020, which gather in 4 clusters in the counties with more housing units. For vegetation cover changes, the pattern is less obvious: deer observations cluster in both regions with high and low destruction. Units: Number of iNaturalist deer observation records per county. Limitation: There were fewer data for 2010 to 2015, so we decided to add all these years up and treat the sum as the pre-development deer distribution. Also, the increase in deer observation may not correlated to development itself, but the increase of people visiting the area and thus seeing more deer.

ANOVA

model_dev <- aov(log(observation) ~ period + development + period*development, data = df_deer_in_NC)
TukeyHSD(model_dev)
##   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
##     95% family-wise confidence level
## 
## Fit: aov(formula = log(observation) ~ period + development + period * development, data = df_deer_in_NC)
## 
## $period
##                   diff       lwr        upr p adj
## before-after -1.120459 -1.408083 -0.8328343     0
## 
## $development
##             diff       lwr       upr     p adj
## yes-no 0.5288883 0.2311184 0.8266582 0.0005809
## 
## $`period:development`
##                            diff        lwr         upr     p adj
## before:no-after:no   -1.0108957 -1.6355211 -0.38627026 0.0002501
## after:yes-after:no    0.6666541  0.1052392  1.22806892 0.0127487
## before:yes-after:no  -0.6036687 -1.1328608 -0.07447659 0.0183030
## after:yes-before:no   1.6775498  1.0948222  2.26027735 0.0000000
## before:yes-before:no  0.4072270 -0.1445239  0.95897793 0.2256389
## before:yes-after:yes -1.2703228 -1.7493413 -0.79130422 0.0000000
fit_dev <- model_dev$fitted
res_dev <- model_dev$res

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
boxplot(observation ~ development+period, data = df_deer_in_NC)
qqnorm(res_dev, datax = TRUE)
qqline(res_dev, col = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(x = seq(1:length(res_dev)), y = res_dev, xlab="Order", ylab="Residuals")
lines(x = seq(1:length(res_dev)), y = res_dev)
abline(0,0)
plot(fit_dev, res_dev, xlab="Fitted Values", ylab="Residuals")

model_forest <- aov(log(observation) ~ period + forest + period*forest, data = df_deer_in_NC)
summary(model_forest)
##                Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value   Pr(>F)    
## period          1  54.62   54.62  62.355 3.31e-13 ***
## forest          1  13.51   13.51  15.423 0.000124 ***
## period:forest   1   6.82    6.82   7.782 0.005876 ** 
## Residuals     171 149.79    0.88                     
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 222 observations deleted due to missingness
TukeyHSD(model_forest)
##   Tukey multiple comparisons of means
##     95% family-wise confidence level
## 
## Fit: aov(formula = log(observation) ~ period + forest + period * forest, data = df_deer_in_NC)
## 
## $period
##                   diff       lwr        upr p adj
## before-after -1.120459 -1.400545 -0.8403728     0
## 
## $forest
##               diff       lwr        upr     p adj
## inc-dec -0.7573773 -1.143998 -0.3707567 0.0001564
## 
## $`period:forest`
##                             diff        lwr        upr     p adj
## before:dec-after:dec  -1.3829640 -1.7866525 -0.9792756 0.0000000
## after:inc-after:dec   -1.2042706 -1.8532504 -0.5552908 0.0000191
## before:inc-after:dec  -1.4363390 -2.3016455 -0.5710326 0.0001626
## after:inc-before:dec   0.1786935 -0.4513465  0.8087334 0.8825235
## before:inc-before:dec -0.0533750 -0.9045687  0.7978188 0.9984622
## before:inc-after:inc  -0.2320685 -1.2234015  0.7592646 0.9296296
fit_forest <- model_forest$fitted
res_forest <- model_forest$res

par(mfrow=c(2,2))
boxplot(observation ~ forest+period, data = df_deer_in_NC)
qqnorm(res_forest, datax = TRUE)
qqline(res_forest, col = "red", lwd = 2)
plot(x = seq(1:length(res_forest)), y = res_forest, xlab="Order", ylab="Residuals")
lines(x = seq(1:length(res_forest)), y = res_forest)
abline(0,0)
plot(fit_forest, res_forest, xlab="Fitted Values", ylab="Residuals")

ANOVA analysis

Question: Are white-tailed deer observations distributed across North Carolina counties significantly different between counties with different development rate? We marked the deer observations from 2010-2015 as pre-development and the data from 2020 as post-development. To fit the ANOVA assumptions better, according to the validity plots, the data is natural log transformed. For housing units, development, period, and their interaction are all significant on deer observation. The Tukey test shows that before the development, the deer observation does not have a significant difference in distribution across the counties. This is the only insignificant case. By contrast, after the development, the deer observation shows a significant difference in distribution across the counties with high and low development. For vegetation cover, forest clearing, period, and their interaction are all significant on deer observation. The Tukey test shows that vegetation cover before development does not have a significant difference on deer observation distribution. However, counties with decreased vegetation cover has a significant difference on deer observation distribution before and after the development. Moreover, after the development, the level of vegetation destruction is significant on deer observation distribution.
